summary: Describes a background file transfer service built on the third-party transfer model of FTP, with no new protocols. It aims to stimulate discussion on new modes of Internet service.

plainLanguage.summary: You hand a courier a job and walk away. The courier moves your files between two computers in the background, so you don't have to wait.

questions: how does third-party ftp transfer work
how does bftp handle network failures
subtitle: Asynchronous file transfers with automatic retries and email notification.

tldr.problem: Interactive file transfers tie up users and fail if the network is congested or hosts are temporarily down. Internet congestion and unreliability make foreground FTP problematic for large transfers.
tldr.mechanism: BFTP uses a user interface to submit transfer requests to a daemon that queues them and executes transfers asynchronously, retrying with exponential backoff if they fail, and notifying the user by email when complete.
tldr.outcome: Users can submit transfers and walk away; the system handles retries and reports results through email, making large transfers practical on unreliable networks.

facts.label: Retry strategy
facts.value: Exponential backoff, e.g., 10 min to 4 hours

facts.label: FTP protocol commands
facts.value: USER, PASS, PASV, PORT, RETR, STOR, STOU, CWD, NLST, MODE, STRU, TYPE, QUIT

today: RFC 1068 is Unknown status and has not been obsoleted. BFTP demonstrated the feasibility of background file transfer on the Internet, though it never became a standard part of widespread practice. Modern systems use different approaches for asynchronous transfer, such as batch job queuing systems or protocol-specific solutions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Background File Transfer Program (BFTP) is an asynchronous file transfer service built on the third-party transfer model of the File Transfer Protocol (FTP). Unlike foreground FTP where a user runs an interactive client and waits for the transfer to complete, BFTP lets users submit transfers to a daemon that executes them in the background.

The Internet in the late 1980s was increasingly subject to congestion, long delays during peak hours, and unpredictable outages of hosts and networks. BFTP addresses these problems by eliminating the need for a user to wait in real time. A user submits transfer parameters once, and the system retries repeatedly until the transfer succeeds or reaches a limit, reporting the result by email.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of sitting at a computer waiting for a file transfer to finish, you can describe what you want moved and let a background program handle it, even if it takes many tries.

sections.title: The BFTP Architecture
sections.content:
BFTP has two main components. The user interface program (bftp) collects transfer parameters from the user: source host and login, destination host and login, file names, and optional settings for transfer mode and timing. The user submits these to a request queue. The FTC daemon (File Transfer Control) reads queued requests and executes them, handling retries and sending completion notifications by email.

Both components must run on the same BFTP control host, which is often different from the source or destination hosts. The user interface can be run directly on any host where the user has privileges, or accessed remotely via a Telnet connection to the BFTP well-known port 152. This lets any Internet user submit transfers without installing BFTP locally.

Users can set a transfer start time (defaulting to immediate), specify retry intervals starting at 10 minutes and doubling to a maximum such as 4 hours (exponential backoff), and limit the number of retries. They also supply a keyword for authentication; this weak scheme lets users later find or cancel their own requests by keyword.
sections.plainLanguage: You use a program to describe the file move and when to try it. That program tells a background courier to deliver the job, and the courier tries again and again until it works or gives up.

sections.title: File Transfer Mechanics
sections.content:
BFTP uses the server-to-server model from FTP. The FTC daemon opens FTP control connections to the source and destination hosts and instructs their FTP servers to transfer the file between them. Neither the user's client nor the BFTP control host itself transfers the actual data; the two FTP servers do, directly or through the bridge host's network.

BFTP can handle multiple files in a single request using wildcards. It sends an NLST command to the source host with a pattern (e.g., foo*) to get a matching list of files, then executes separate transfer operations for each file, transferring to a destination with the same name. BFTP must support all FTP file types and transfer modes (ASCII, EBCDIC, image, stream, block, compress) and structures (file, record, page) because it may bridge between hosts with different capabilities.

The protocol uses standard FTP commands: USER, PASS, ACCT, PASV, PORT, RETR, STOR, STOU, CWD, NLST, MODE, STRU, TYPE, and QUIT. It works around servers that don't support optional commands like CWD by constructing full paths instead. The daemon requires at least one of the two hosts to support the PASV (passive) command.
sections.plainLanguage: The courier doesn't carry the files; instead, it tells two post offices where the mail is and where it should go, and they send it directly between each other.

sections.title: Reliability and Retries
sections.content:
BFTP's core function is reliable end-to-end delivery. When a transfer fails temporarily (e.g., a broken TCP connection), the daemon logs the failure and retries after a timeout period. The retry interval starts short—say 10 minutes—and doubles with each attempt until it reaches a maximum, such as 4 hours. This exponential backoff strategy balances the urgency of transfers against the overhead of frequent retries.

For multiple-file requests, the daemon saves the file list returned by the first successful NLST command. This list determines exactly which files will be transferred; later additions to the source directory are ignored. The daemon maintains a transfer status pointer and, on each retry, transfers only the files that have not yet succeeded. When all individual transfers succeed, a permanent failure occurs, or the retry limit is reached, the daemon sends a completion notification to the user's mailbox with the status of each file.

The RFC notes that regarding a multiple-file transfer as a single atomic operation would be impractical—deleting successfully transferred files on retry would be inefficient and impossible if the communication path is broken.
sections.plainLanguage: If delivery fails, the courier waits a bit and tries again, waiting longer each time. It tracks which files arrived and doesn't re-send those on the next attempt.

sections.title: User Interface and Control
sections.content:
BFTP's user interface is modeled on the TOPS-20 operating system and provides extensive help and defaulting. Users can enter ? for a list of commands, help for explanations, or help [command] for specific help. The prompt command walks through basic parameters: transfer mode (copy, move, or delete source), FTP type, source and destination hosts with logins, directories, and filenames.

BFTP supports three modes of operation. Background operation uses the submit command to queue the transfer with the daemon. Foreground verification uses verify to check that both hosts are reachable, credentials work, and files exist before submitting for background execution. Foreground operation uses transfer to perform the transfer immediately, bypassing the queue.

Users can list all parameters with status, reset to defaults with clear, and save or load request sets to files. When submitting, users enter a return mailbox and a keyword; this keyword can later be used with find to retrieve request status or cancel to stop execution. A Sun workstation version, bftptool, provides a window-based interface with form-style parameter entry and mouse-based help.
sections.plainLanguage: You answer a series of questions about where the files are and where they should go, then pick a simple command to submit the job or check on it later by name.
